name: How much contingency should I set aside for a custom home build?

mainEntity.name: How much contingency should I budget for a single-family home construction project?
mainEntity.text: How much contingency should I budget for a single-family home construction project?

acceptedAnswer.text: A contingency reserve is essential because no early estimate captures every site condition or future change. In single-family home construction, surprises can come from soil conditions, permit comments, utility work, material price changes, or owner-driven upgrades. A project without contingency is more likely to stall or shrink in scope when something changes. The amount should reflect how complex the lot and design are: flatter, simpler projects may need less buffer than hillside, luxury, or heavily customized homes. Owners should treat contingency as protected money, not spending money for upgrades. It is also smart to distinguish between design contingency, construction contingency, and allowance overages so the budget is easier to track. The best time to decide on contingency is before plans are finalized, because once construction starts, the cost of change rises quickly.
acceptedAnswer.description: A contingency reserve is usually needed because site conditions, material changes, and design revisions can increase costs during construction. Many owners set aside a meaningful percentage of the project budget so they can handle surprises without stopping work or cutting scope.
